name: David Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a wheel loader at a large mine, moving ore onto the haul line and watching the foot routes every minute. I'm 58 and still junior on this crew, with a lot to learn about the newer controls. I like the moment a load settles properly in the bucket. The tablet inspections run long, and a camera cable on my loader keeps losing its connection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a quicker inspection form is welcome if it means less time at the tablet after a shift. The loader still needs a person watching the bucket and the people walking near it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Ines and I have around three months of expenses put by, and we still pay on the house. I can live with a little software change, but I don't call those bills harmless just because AI stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader shifts and show the fitter the camera cable that drops out. In the first year, I'd use any AI-assisted inspection screen the mine brings in and put part of each full month's pay toward the roof account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly calm about this version because my actual seat and wage look steady. The house costs still sit in the back of my mind; they don't vanish with the AI headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you lose time on an ordinary shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose cable on the loader's camera gives me a blank screen now and then, so I stop and call the fitter. No program saves time when the basic camera won't stay on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and Ines do with a steady month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Ines puts the house payment first, then we try to leave something in the savings account. Our grown son pays his own rent now, which helps, but the roof still needs attention.

say: I'd welcome **quicker inspection forms** if they give operators more time near the equipment.
Our loader still needs **human eyes** around the bucket and walking routes.
think: I can handle **small software** changes after somebody shows they work.
My wife and I still have a **house payment** and a roof needing repair.
do: Keep working **loader shifts** and report the failing camera cable.
Use the mine's **AI-assisted inspection screen** after a practical demonstration.
Put money from full months into our **roof account**.
feel: **Calm** about his job, while ordinary house costs remain on his mind.
S0.quote: No program saves time when the basic camera won't stay on.
fieldNote: David ties useful technology to a **working camera** and a practical improvement in inspection time.
The household's **three-month cushion** leaves room for modest repairs but not carefree spending.

steps.text: Keep operating the loader and report its failing camera cable
Use the mine AI-assisted inspection screen after a practical demonstration
Put money from full pay months into the roof account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch and ordering are where the mine will try software first, because that's mostly screens already. I would ask the foreman to show operators any changes on the machine, not just email instructions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in dispatch could lose hours, and that may make our shift patterns strange. My loader is physical work, but the slower spread of robots means I should learn what the mine actually installs before claiming I'm safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the foreman for a demonstration of any new loader screen, then keep running my shifts. In the first year, I'd take a mine-funded session on new controls if it covers our actual equipment, and check the rota each month for lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy because the first losses could be in rooms I don't work in, then reach our rota. Having seen the weighbridge change go all right, I don't feel beaten by a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has changed at the mine before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the new weighbridge screen came in, my colleague Mara showed me twice and I got it. I use a phone assistant now and then to check a term, but I don't trust it to tell me whether a haul road is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend money on training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a course sold with promises about future jobs. I'd take a mine-funded session on the loader controls if it is tied to the equipment we use next season.

say: I'd say **dispatch and ordering** will change before the loader seat does.
Operators need **hands-on instruction** when software changes the machines.
think: I expect **dispatch hours** could shrink, with knock-on changes to our shifts.
My **loader work** faces robots later, so I need facts about the mine's equipment plans.
do: Ask the foreman for a **loader-screen demonstration** and keep taking shifts.
Take **mine-funded controls training** if it covers equipment we actually use.
Check the **monthly rota** for a fall in assigned hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about a thinner rota, but confident he can learn demonstrated controls.
S1.quote: I don't trust it to tell me whether a haul road is safe.
fieldNote: David's **weighbridge experience** makes him willing to try new controls when a colleague demonstrates them.
He sees **dispatch losses** as a possible route to changed operator hours, despite the physical loader work.

steps.text: Keep running assigned loader shifts and ask for a screen demonstration
Take mine-funded controls training if it covers current equipment
Check the monthly rota for any drop in assigned hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift crew full thinking AI by 2028 would hit dispatch before our loader, and that robots would come around 2031. I'd ask the manager for a date and a plan, because the second part could take my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 60 when the thinking system arrives and 63 when the robot can do the bucket work. The mine could keep us for a while, but three months' savings and an unfinished house loan cannot cover a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the loader through 2029 and ask management for its robot timetable. That first year, I'd record every offered shift, call two nearby mines about openings, and defer the kitchen cabinets to protect our cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed because this has a date near enough for me to count down. I can make calls, but I cannot make another mine hire me at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, the first year after the thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still run the loader, ask to see the machine schedule, and write down every shift I am offered. I would also call two nearby mines about operator openings, even though I cannot know they will have them in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Ines that our son is independent, but we still owe on the house. We'd delay replacing the kitchen cabinets and keep the roof money separate from everyday bills.

say: I'd tell the crew **2028 AI** takes thinking work first, with loader-capable robots around 2031.
We need a **machine schedule** before operators have to guess about their wages.
think: At **63 in 2031**, I may lose loader hours before our house loan is paid.
Our **three-month cushion** cannot carry us through an unknown wage gap.
do: Keep **operating the loader** through 2029 while robots have not arrived.
Request the **robot timetable** and record each shift offered.
Call **two nearby mines** about operator openings.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely wage gap near age 63 and an unfinished house loan.
S2.quote: I can make calls, but I cannot make another mine hire me at 63.
fieldNote: David would still do **paid loader work** after 2028 AGI while anticipating robot competition around 2031.
His search for **nearby openings** is an inquiry, not an assumed offer or guaranteed replacement income.

steps.text: Keep operating the loader through the first year after 2028 AI
Request the robot timetable and record offered shifts
Call two nearby mines about operator openings
Defer replacing kitchen cabinets to protect cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us time to see whether the mine is buying machines or only talking. At 63 in 2031, I might still have three years before robots can do the loader work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 in 2034, I would like to slow down, but I do not know that I could stop. I would use the warning to find the real balance on the house and our retirement accounts, rather than turn a hoped-for date into a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader shifts and ask for the mine's purchase plan, not just a rumour. In the first year after 2031, I'd review our loan and retirement statements with Ines, shadow the fitter only if the mine offers a paid route to training, and check nearby openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I have enough time to make a measured choice. The worry is whether the numbers allow that choice, not whether I can learn one more control panel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes if the warning is five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can ask the mine to let me shadow the fitter who checks the loader sensors, if it offers a proper paid course afterward. I know my way around the machine, but I am not a fitter just because I've watched one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the course isn't offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my seat while it lasts and look at nearby operator vacancies once a year. I wouldn't pay for a technical certificate myself without knowing it leads to an actual job.

say: I'd say **five years** lets operators check whether the mine actually orders robots.
The loader seat may last until **2034**, but its end cannot be assumed away.
think: At **66 in 2034**, I may still need to earn.
I need real **house and retirement figures** before deciding when to leave paid work.
do: Keep **loader shifts** while the mine still assigns them.
Review **loan and retirement statements** with Ines in 2032.
Shadow the **loader fitter** if the mine offers a paid training route.
feel: **Anxious** about income after robots, with time to check the figures and training route.
S3.quote: I am not a fitter just because I've watched one.
fieldNote: He sees five years as time to verify **machine purchases** and his own financial position.
His interest in maintenance is **conditional** on paid training; watching a fitter alone does not qualify him.

steps.text: Keep working assigned loader shifts through the first year after 2031 AI
Review house loan and retirement statements with Ines in 2032
Shadow the fitter if the mine offers a paid training route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should be enough for an employer to say what machines it intends to buy and what happens to drivers. I'd be 68 in 2036, but the loader robots come around 2039 when I'd be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have left by 2039, yet I won't claim that until Ines and I know what our retirement income will be. Thinking AI in 2036 could change dispatch, but the bucket work remains mine until the hands-on machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loader job, order our retirement statements, and use full-pay months to pay extra against the house loan. If I'm still employed in 2037, I'd keep taking shifts and apply for nearby equipment work if our accounts say we still need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but a decade lets me test the figures rather than stare at a deadline. It would still hurt to be pushed out of a job I've learned just as I get ready to leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do now with a decade to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for our retirement statements and set a date to review them with Ines each year. I'd keep my loader job and use full-pay months to clear more of the house loan, rather than buy a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Suppose you're still working in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd keep driving the loader if I am fit and the mine still has shifts. If our accounts show a shortfall, I'd apply for suitable equipment work at another nearby mine rather than wait for the robot date.

say: I'd ask the mine for **purchase dates** and a plain plan for drivers.
At **68 in 2036**, I might still need loader wages.
think: I cannot count on **retirement income** until Ines and I see the figures.
I may still drive after **2036 AI**, with hands-on robots due around 2039.
do: Keep working **loader shifts** if fit and assigned in 2037.
Pay extra against the **house loan** from full-pay months.
Apply for **nearby equipment work** if accounts show wages remain necessary.
feel: **Uneasy** about a possible wage gap, though the longer warning gives him choices.
S4.quote: I'd be 68 in 2036, but the loader robots come around 2039 when I'd be 71.
fieldNote: David expects **thinking AI** to reach dispatch in 2036 before robots can operate loaders around 2039.
He ties 2037 **job applications** to a measured income shortfall, rather than declaring retirement at 68.

steps.text: Keep taking loader shifts in 2037 if fit and assigned
Pay extra against the house loan from full-pay months
Apply for nearby equipment work if accounts show wages are needed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robot date around 2031 could arrive while I still have house debt. A written machine plan, paid training on real equipment, and a clear statement of our retirement money would let me judge whether to keep operating or apply elsewhere. I would not call any other mine a sure job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the older junior operators when a new control comes in. My colleague Mara got me through the weighbridge screen by showing me twice, and that mattered more than the manual.

headlineQuote: I know my way around the machine, but I am not a fitter just because I've watched one.
portrait: David is a **58-year-old junior** wheel-loader operator who trusts equipment he has seen work in practice.
He and his wife Ines have **three months saved**, a house loan and a roof that needs attention.
He sometimes uses a **phone assistant**, but wants practical demonstrations before relying on mine technology.
He fears **2031 robots** could end loader wages while debt remains, and checks nearby jobs without assuming an offer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because the 2031 robot date could arrive while the house loan remains.
whatWouldHelp: A written **machine plan** and paid training on real equipment would let him judge his next job move.
Clear **retirement figures** would show whether he and Ines can manage without loader wages.
